common_name: Slater's Crimson China Rose (Original Founding Deep-Red China Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Slater's Crimson China is one of the four founding China roses introduced to Europe in the late 1700s, credited with bringing true red color and repeat bloom into Western rose breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Slater's Crimson China, imported to Europe around 1792, is one of the four founding China roses and holds enormous historical significance as the source of true velvety crimson-red color and reliable repeat bloom in Western rose breeding, traits absent from the once-blooming European roses grown before its arrival. It bears semi-double, deep crimson flowers with little fragrance, blooming in flushes nearly continuously through the growing season on a tough, easygoing shrub with excellent heat tolerance. Prune lightly to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; it needs little other care once established.
sources: American Rose Society — China Rose Class Descriptions
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Old Garden Rose Collections

common_name: Hermosa Rose (Clear Soft Pink Globular China-Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Hermosa, introduced in 1840, bears clear soft-pink, globular double blooms on a small, tidy China-Bourbon type bush.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Hermosa, introduced in France in 1840, bears clear, soft pink, globular double blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on a small, tidy, well-behaved bush blending traits of the China and Bourbon classes, flowering in flushes nearly continuously through the growing season. Its compact size and reliable, gentle color have made it a long-standing favorite for small gardens, edging, and container culture where larger old garden roses would be impractical. Prune lightly to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; it needs little other care once established.
sources: American Rose Society — China Rose Class Descriptions
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Old Garden Rose Collections

common_name: Autumn Damask Rose (Rare Repeat-Flowering Fragrant Pink Damask)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumn Damask is the rare repeat-flowering damask rose, blooming again lightly in fall.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Autumn Damask is historically remarkable as one of the very few old European roses capable of a genuine, if lighter, second bloom in fall, a trait most old garden rose classes lack entirely, bearing loosely double, clear pink, intensely fragrant flowers in both flushes. Its ancient origins and repeat-blooming trait made it an important ancestor in the eventual development of modern repeat-flowering rose classes. Deadhead the spring flush to encourage the fall repeat, and prune lightly in late winter to shape.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Kazanlik is the classic damask rose grown commercially in Bulgaria's Rose Valley for rose oil (attar of roses) production.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Kazanlik is the historic damask rose grown at commercial scale in Bulgaria's famed Rose Valley for centuries to distill attar of roses, the concentrated rose oil at the heart of the perfume industry, bearing loosely double, soft pink blooms with an intensely rich, classic rose fragrance considered among the finest of any rose. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably cold-hardy and disease-resistant, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Celsiana Rose (Semi-Double Light Pink Fragrant Damask)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Celsiana bears semi-double, light pink blooms with a graceful, informal form and strong fragrance.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Celsiana bears large, semi-double, soft light-pink blooms with translucent, papery petals and prominent golden stamens, opening in a graceful, informal, loosely cupped form with a strong, classic damask fragrance considered among the best of the class. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Leda Rose (Painted Damask, Creamy White Edged Crimson)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Leda, known as the Painted Damask, bears creamy white petals edged in crimson, most vivid on the buds.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Leda, popularly called the Painted Damask, bears creamy white double blooms delicately edged in crimson-red, the contrasting rim most vivid and vibrant on the tightly furled buds and softening slightly as the flower fully opens, a distinctive hand-painted look unique among damask roses. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Botzaris Rose (Very Double Quartered White with Green Button Eye)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Botzaris bears very double, quartered white blooms with a small green button eye at the center.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Botzaris bears very double, densely petaled white blooms arranged in a distinctive quartered pattern with a small, tidy green button eye visible at the very center when fully open, a refined, formal flower structure prized among damask rose collectors, carrying the class's characteristic strong, sweet fragrance. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: York and Lancaster Rose (Historic Blush-White Splashed Pink Damask)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; York and Lancaster bears blush-white flowers often splashed or striped with pink, historically tied to the Wars of the Roses legend.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. York and Lancaster carries centuries of English history in its name, its blush-white blooms irregularly splashed and striped with pink in a pattern said to symbolize the warring houses of York and Lancaster, with individual flowers on the same bush sometimes appearing nearly solid white or solid pink alongside the classic bicolor pattern. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Rose de Rescht (Persian Compact Fuchsia-Magenta Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rose de Rescht is a Persian-origin Portland rose popularized in the West by rose historian Nancy Lindsay, prized for its compact size and intense fragrance.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Rose de Rescht, of Persian origin and popularized in Western gardens by rose historian Nancy Lindsay, bears densely double, vivid fuchsia-magenta flowers with an intense, rich fragrance on a notably compact bush, one of the smaller-growing Portland roses and well suited to a mixed border or smaller garden where larger old garden roses would overwhelm the space. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Duchess of Portland Rose (Original Namesake Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Duchess of Portland is the original namesake rose of the entire Portland class, bearing bright crimson-scarlet semi-double flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Duchess of Portland is the original rose that gave its name to the entire Portland class of old garden roses, bearing bright, clear crimson-scarlet, semi-double flowers held close against the foliage on short stems, a distinctive tight, ruffled foliage collar just beneath each bloom being a hallmark trait of the class it founded. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Marchesa Boccella (Blush-Pink Fragrant Quartered Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Marchesa Boccella, introduced in 1842, bears soft blush-pink, very fragrant, quartered double blooms.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Marchesa Boccella, introduced in France in 1842, bears soft blush-pink, very double blooms arranged in the classic quartered pattern with an intense, sweet fragrance considered among the finest of the Portland class, opening on an upright, well-branched shrub. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Yolande d'Aragon Rose (Deep Pink-Magenta Fragrant Tall Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Yolande d'Aragon bears deep pink-magenta, full, fragrant blooms on a taller Portland shrub than most in its class.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Yolande d'Aragon bears full, richly fragrant, deep pink-to-magenta blooms on a taller, more vigorous shrub than most Portland roses, which are typically compact, giving it more presence at the back of a mixed border. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Rose du Roi (Historic Bright Red Portland, Hybrid Perpetual Ancestor)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rose du Roi, introduced in 1815, is historically important as an ancestor of the later Hybrid Perpetual rose class.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Rose du Roi, introduced in France in 1815, bears bright, fragrant red double flowers and holds significant historical importance as a key ancestor in the development of the later Hybrid Perpetual rose class, which dominated nineteenth-century rose breeding and eventually gave rise to the modern hybrid tea. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Lady Hillingdon Rose (Apricot-Yellow Tea Rose with Plum-Colored New Growth)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Lady Hillingdon, introduced in 1910, bears apricot-yellow tea rose blooms with distinctive plum-colored young stems and foliage, also known through a popular climbing sport.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3 to 3.5 feet apart. Lady Hillingdon, introduced in England in 1910, bears elegant, loosely double, apricot-yellow blooms with a rich tea fragrance, distinguished from other tea roses by its striking plum-purple young stems and new foliage that provide ornamental interest even between flushes. Like other tea roses it flowers almost continuously from spring to frost and shows good resistance to blackspot in the humid Gulf South compared with modern hybrid teas; a vigorous climbing sport of the same cultivar is also widely grown where more height is wanted. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Lady Hillingdon variety notes
